report:
**Conclusion:** For typical knee osteoarthritis, arthroscopy (lavage, “clean-up”/debridement, or removal of degenerative meniscal tissue) does **not** meaningfully improve pain, function, or knee-specific quality of life compared with placebo surgery or good non-operative care. It also exposes patients to surgical and anesthetic risks and recovery time.

This conclusion is supported by placebo-controlled randomized trials: lavage or debridement performed no better than sham surgery, and adding arthroscopy to optimized physical/medical therapy did not improve outcomes in moderate-to-severe OA. A 2022 Cochrane review likewise found little or no clinically important benefit.

Accordingly, a BMJ international guideline makes a **strong recommendation against** arthroscopy for nearly all degenerative knee disease—including people with imaging-confirmed OA, degenerative meniscal tears, or common “mechanical” symptoms such as clicking/catching.

This does not address a different situation: an orthopedist may consider urgent arthroscopy for a **true locked knee** (inability to straighten it), or for an acute traumatic injury/loose body—not as treatment for OA itself. Discuss persistent symptoms with a clinician; exercise-based rehabilitation, weight management where applicable, and pain-management options are generally preferred first.
